title: The Fixed-Pie Assumption
text:
In the late 1980s Leigh Thompson and Reid Hastie studied what negotiators believe about the other side, and how those beliefs shape the deals they reach. They set up simulated negotiations between pairs of students, such as a buyer and a seller of a car, covering several issues at once.

The cases were designed so that the two sides did not want opposite things on every issue. On some issues one side cared a lot and the other cared little, which allowed trades that would leave both better off. On at least one issue, both sides actually wanted the same outcome. The researchers asked negotiators, before and after bargaining, what they thought the other party wanted.

Most negotiators assumed that the other side's interests were directly opposed to their own on every issue, so that anything good for one meant equal loss for the other. Thompson and Hastie called this the fixed-pie perception. It formed early, often within the first few minutes, and it shaped the outcomes. Negotiators who held it reached worse joint agreements, missing trades that would have helped both. Some even settled on outcomes that were worse for both parties on the very issues where they agreed, because each assumed the other wanted the opposite and gave in on it as a concession.

Those who realized during the negotiation that interests could differ in importance reached much better agreements for both sides.
lesson: In a negotiation, do not assume the other side wants the opposite of you on everything. Ask what matters most to them, and share what matters most to you, to find trades that help both.
source: Thompson, L., and Hastie, R. (1990). Social perception in negotiation. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 47(1), 98-123.
